UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company                       )
                                                                )
v.                                                              )                        Docket No. EL26-38-000
                                                                )
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.                  )


                           MOTION TO INTERVENE AND PROTEST OF
                            THE MICHIGAN ATTORNEY GENERAL

          Pursuant to Rules 211 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”
or the “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel,
on behalf of the People of the State of Michigan, seeks to intervene as a party in the docket and
submits this protest in response to the Complaint filed by Southern Indiana Gas and Electric
Company d/b/a CenterPoint Energy Indiana South (“SIGE” or the “Company”) requesting the
Commission require adoption of a cost recovery mechanism for costs to comply with the
Department of Energy Order 2 issued pursuant to Section 202(c) of Federal Power Act (“FPA”) to
prevent the scheduled retirement of SIGE’s F.B. Culley Generating Station Unit 2 (the “Culley
Unit”).

    I.    MOTION TO INTERVENE

          The Michigan Attorney General, 3 on behalf of the people of the State of Michigan, moves
to intervene in this proceeding. The People of the State of Michigan have a direct interest in the
outcome of this proceeding as the households and businesses of Michigan, along with the State
itself, may face higher electricity bills as a result of the cost recovery mechanism at issue in the
proceeding.



1
          18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025).
2
          Department of Energy Order No. 202-25-13 (December 23, 2025) (the “DOE Order”).
3
          See MCL 14.28 (“The attorney general . . . may, when in [her] own judgment the interests of the state require
it, intervene in and appear for the people of this state in any other court or tribunal, in any cause or matter, civil or
criminal, in which the people of this state may be a party or interested.”). See also, In re Certified Question, 465 Mich
537, 543-545, 638 N.W.2d 409 (2002); See also, Gremore v. Peoples Community Hospital Authority, 8 Mich. App. 56,
153 N.W.2d 377 (1967); See also, People v. O’Hara, 278 Mich. 281, 270 N.W. 298 (1936).

                                                           1
     II.    SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

           The Michigan Attorney General requests that the Commission deny the complaint, because
the underlying DOE Order justifying cost recovery is ultra vires, and, absent a valid legal
obligation to operate pursuant to FPA Section 202(c), the imposition of the costs of operating the
Culley Unit on ratepayers pursuant to FPA Sections 205 or 206: (i) is not just and reasonable and
is unduly discriminatory or preferential; and (ii) violates the filed rate doctrine. If the Commission
is not inclined to deny the Complaint on the merits, the Commission should instead use the
discretion afforded by FPA Section 202(c) to dismiss the complaint without prejudice until the
scope and legal validity of the DOE Order is settled.

           If the Commission does not reject SIGE’s request, the Commission must, at minimum,
require that the cost recovery mechanism incorporate certain customer safeguards, including
provisions to facilitate a refund of the unlawful charges to customers (in the event the DOE Order
is invalidated) and to limit recovery to only those costs that are necessary to operate under the
limits imposed by the DOE Order (in the event the DOE Order is not invalidated). Additionally,
in order to comply with cost causation principles, the Commission must require cost allocation on
a load ratio share basis across the MISO region. The DOE Order asserts an obligation under federal
law to make the Culley Unit available to operate on the basis of a purported region-wide
emergency, not local conditions, and accordingly any “benefit” of such operation accrues region-
wide.

    III.   PROTEST
           a. The Commission should deny SIGE’s Complaint because the DOE Order is ultra
              vires and the cost recovery mechanism is unnecessary—and unjust,
              unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory—absent a valid FPA 202(c) order.

           SIGE requests imposition of its proposed cost recovery mechanism primarily on the basis
of FPA Sections 202(c), 306, and 309. 4 However, SIGE itself does not allege that keeping the
Culley Unit available and operating it during the period of the Order is necessary for resource
adequacy or reliability. Indeed, SIGE’s Complaint acknowledges that MISO studied the Culley
Unit pursuant to its Attachment Y process, under which MISO would have determined that



4
           SIGE’s Complaint at 1.

                                                  2
 retirement of the unit would not result in violations of applicable reliability criteria. 5 SIGE’s
Complaint also acknowledges that such retirement was approved through Indiana’s state-regulated
Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) processes. 6 Further emphasizing the soundness of the MISO and
state-level resource adequacy planning, the most recent North American Electricity Reliability
Corporation’s (“NERC’s”) 2025-2026 Winter Reliability Assessment identifies MISO as a “normal
risk” for the winter months, the lowest category of risk designation. 7 The 2025-2026 Winter
Reliability Assessment also finds that MISO’s anticipated and projected resources exceed the
reference margin level. 8 Because substantial evidence shows that the Culley Unit is not necessary
to ensure reliable operation during the period of the DOE Order, in MISO Zones 1-7 or elsewhere,
forcing MISO customers to bear the costs of the Culley Unit’s operation is not just and reasonable.

         Cost recovery here under Sections 205/206 of the FPA would also violate the filed rate
doctrine. 9 SIGE has filed its complaint precisely because the MISO tariff does not permit cost
recovery for the costs it has incurred to make the Culley Unit available to operate. If the DOE
Order is struck down by the courts, the Commission would have no choice but to refund any
charges to MISO’s customers because even “the Commission itself has no power to alter a rate
retroactively.” 10

         The Commission’s authority to impose these retroactive and unjust and unreasonable costs
on MISO customers therefore hinges solely on the validity of the DOE Order. But the DOE Order
is ultra vires. Crucially, no evidence substantiates the DOE Order’s determination that the MISO


5

MISO to suspend operation of Culley Unit 2 effective December 31, 2025; MISO approved the request on June 3,
2025, after performing its reliability analysis.”).
6
         See, id. at 9 – 10.
7

2025), https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/assessments/nerc_wra_2025.pdf, at 6 fig. 1.
8

amount of reserve capacity in the system above the forecasted peak demand that is needed to ensure sufficient supply
to meet peak loads.” Id. at 41. MISO’s reference margin level is substantially higher than that of any other region in
North America. See, id. at 42.
9
          Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 892 F.3d 1223, 1226 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (“The Act also empowers the
Commission to fix or change rates and charges, but only prospectively. 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a). When a utility wishes to
alter the rates it charges, it must provide sixty-days’ notice to the Commission and file new rate schedules “stating
plainly the change or changes to be made in the schedule or schedules then in force and the time when the change or
changes will go into effect.” Id. § 824d(d).”).
10
         Arkansas Louisiana Gas Co. v. Hall, 453 U.S. 571, 578 (1981).

                                                            3
 region faces an emergency during the period of the DOE Order. As discussed above, NERC’s most
recent winter 2025-2026 assessment plainly contradicts any assertion of an emergency during the
period of the DOE Order, and instead reinforces the soundness of the MISO and state-level
processes for planning the Culley Unit’s retirement. Likewise, the relevant grid operator (here,
MISO) has not requested this DOE Order as necessary.

        The Michigan Attorney General has further identified a litany of other points demonstrating
the invalidity of the DOE Order in a Motion to Intervene and Petition for Rehearing filed January
22, 2025 (the “Petition for Rehearing”, attached hereto as Appendix A); the arguments raised in
that Petition for Rehearing are incorporated herein by reference. If DOE grants rehearing, the scope
of operation of the Culley unit and, correspondingly, SIGE’s costs to comply with the DOE Order,
may change materially.

        The Commission should thus deny SIGE’s complaint. If the Commission is not inclined
to deny the complaint on its merits, it should use the discretion afforded by FPA Section 202(c)—
which makes clear that issuing an order to prescribe compensation or reimbursement is
discretionary, not mandatory, and sets no timeline in which such matters must be resolved 11—to
deny the Complaint without prejudice as prematurely filed. Given that the DOE Order is invalid,
and the potential that the Department of Energy may change the scope of cost recovery on
rehearing, the Commission has good cause to defer its determination of a just and reasonable cost
recovery mechanism until these issues concerning the scope and validity of the DOE Order are
resolved. A delay is appropriate as a safeguard against the potential imposition of unjust and
unreasonable charges, and to avoid administrative inefficiency that would result if the DOE Order
changes in scope or is invalidated, necessitating refunds.

        b. If the Commission does not deny the Complaint, it must impose certain limits on
           the cost recovery mechanism in order to ensure just and reasonable
           compensation.

        If the Commission grants the complaint, the Commission must modify SIGE’s proposed
cost recovery mechanism to ensure any charges pursuant to it are just and reasonable. Even when
acting under Section 202(c), the Commission is only empowered to prescribe compensation or

11
        FPA Section 202(c)(1) (“the Commission, after hearing held either before or after such order takes effect,
may prescribe by supplemental order such terms as it finds to be just and reasonable, including the compensation or
reimbursement which should be paid to or by any such party”) (emphasis added).

                                                        4
 reimbursement “it finds to be just and reasonable.” 12 SIGE’s proposed Schedule 13 omits certain
safeguards to limit cost recovery to only costs that are needed to operate consistent with the DOE
Order, and therefore risks violating longstanding Commission cost causation requirements.

        Cost causation principles require that all rates must reflect to some degree the costs actually
caused by the customers who pay them. 14 Assuming arguendo that the DOE Order is valid,
customers are only responsible for the expenditures that are necessary to operate the Culley Unit
for the limited period of operation set forth in the DOE Order and under the conditions imposed
(“economic dispatch” so as “to minimize costs to ratepayers” 15) by the DOE Order; that is the
scope of operation that the DOE Order deems necessary to address the purported emergency, and
circumscribes the scope of “benefits” of operation that customers are responsible to pay for. In
the context of SSR units or the comparable “Reliability-Must-Run” (RMR) units in other RTO/ISO
regions, the Commission has recognized, for example, that if a generation resource recovers from
load the costs of significant upgrades during the term of the SSR or RMR Agreement, but then
rescinds the suspension notice or otherwise returns to service, such expenditures must be
reimbursed to comply with cost causation principles. 16 Absent a protective measure such as a
clawback provision, the Commission has held that an SSR or RMR unit may unjustly and
unreasonably receive a windfall if it forces customers to pay for expenditures that enable the unit
to later return to commercial operation. 17

        For the same reasons, any cost recovery mechanism applicable to the Culley Unit must
include safeguards to limit the scope of cost recovery to only those expenditures necessary for its

13

14

Wisconsin, 150 FERC ¶ 61,104, 61,704 (2015) (“SSR cost allocation should be commensurate with reliability benefits
received from continued operation of an SSR Unit”).

 limited scope of operation under the DOE Order and/or provide a clawback provision to reimburse
customers for all or a portion of costs if the Culley Unit continues to operate beyond the terms of
the DOE Order. For example, extensive repairs, 18 such as those that might extend beyond the
period of the DOE Order, to render the Culley Unit operational, would be inconsistent with the
DOE Order. Such costs would not be necessary to ensure operation of the unit during the period
of the DOE Order, and accordingly such costs would not be recoverable. On this basis, SIGE
cannot reasonably recover at least the following expenses:

                 a. Delivered cost of consumables inventory on-hand after the end of the period of
                      the DOE Order, including fuel and various materials used in environmental
                      control systems;
                 b. Costs of commodities or equipment to support continued operations that will
                      not be delivered until after the end of the period of the DOE Order.
                 c. Costs of maintenance or repairs that require generating unit shutdown past the
                      end of the period of the DOE Order; and
                 d. Costs of maintenance and repairs other than those strictly necessary to maintain
                      the operational status of the Culley Unit until the end of the period of the DOE
                      Order.

        In addition, the DOE Order requires that MISO “take every step to employ economic
dispatch” of the Cullet Unit in order “to minimize cost to ratepayers.” While the DOE Order lacks
a precise definition of “economic dispatch,” a reasonable interpretation of this requirement must
give meaning to the directive to minimize costs to ratepayers. Any form of commitment and
dispatch that enables the Culley Unit to operate at a net loss in its market operation, given its
operating limits, is inconsistent with the DOE Order. 19 If SIGE self-commits the Culley Unit as a
“Must Run” unit and the resulting dispatch results in a net loss in its market operations over a
period of time in which the unit could have been turned off (because it was committed as Economic
or Emergency), that operation resulting in a net loss cannot constitute “economic dispatch” that




18
          See, e.g., SIGE Complaint at 5, FN15 (“SIGE notes that Culley Unit 2 is currently in a maintenance outage
but is preparing Culley Unit 2 to be offered into the MISO market and to produce energy when dispatched.”).
19
          See as explained in the Motion to Intervene and Protest of the Michigan Attorney General in FERC Docket
No. EL25-90-000, Affidavit of Douglas Jester at PP 10-17.

                                                        6
 “minimizes costs to ratepayers” as required by the DOE Order. 20 Likewise, if costs of repair are
necessary to be operable, those costs must be factored in as a cost of commitment. 21 The operation
of the Culley Unit can only qualify as “economic dispatch” if the net energy value in market
operations before the end of the period of the DOE Order exceeds the cost of commitment
including the necessary repairs. 22

         SIGE’s proposed MISO tariff schedule does not include any language to limit the scope of
recoverable costs to those that are necessary to comply with the DOE Order. The Commission
must direct MISO to incorporate such limits on cost recovery and incorporate other safeguards,
such as a clawback provision, to ensure the mechanism is just and reasonable.

         Finally, the most significant risk that the cost recovery mechanism will impose unjust and
unreasonable costs on customers is the likelihood that the DOE Order is overturned by the courts.
A just and reasonable cost recovery mechanism would facilitate reimbursement of unlawful
retroactive and unjust and unreasonable charges in the event the DOE Order is overturned. 23

         c. To be consistent with cost-causation principles, cost allocation must be RTO-
            wide.

         SIGE proposes cost allocation to MISO Zones 1-7, premised on an assertion that this
reflects the scope and nature of the emergency addressed by the DOE Order. 24 However, it is
incorrect to say that the DOE Order purported to identify reliability risks only in MISO’s northern
and central zones as the basis for the emergency. Any cost allocation must thus be on a load ratio
basis across the entire MISO region in order to meet cost-causation principles.

is illustrative. Unwinding retroactive charges can be tremendously complex and administratively burdensome for the
RTO/ISO. A tariff mechanism to track and reimburse charges could greatly reduce complexity and burden. See

         The language of the DOE Order asserts an emergency throughout the entirety of MISO,25
and it does not limit its assessment of the emergency to particular zones in MISO. The DOE Order’s
only reference to the Northern and Central regions specifically is in the context of the MISO PRA
Auction Results for Planning Year 2025-26. 26 However, Slide 4 of the same document states that
the North/Central zones have a higher effective summer margin at 10.1% compared to the South
zones at 8.7%. 27 To the extent that the DOE Order would be read to establish that an emergency
exists at all, that emergency would extend across the MISO region, and would not be limited to any
particular MISO zones.

        Moreover, assuming arguendo the validity of the DOE Order, then the operation of the
Culley Unit would be necessary to comply with a federal law. Accordingly, the “benefit” of its
operation accrues broadly throughout the region. Under Commission precedent, cost allocation is
roughly commensurate with the benefits where the costs to comply with a law are shared across the
law’s applicable jurisdiction. For example, where New York State law required investment in
certain transmission infrastructure to achieve State policy objectives, the Commission held that it
is consistent with cost causation principles to allocate the costs of those projects on a volumetric
load-ratio share basis across New York State. 28 Following this precedent, the costs of complying
with the DOE Order must be allocated to the whole of the MISO region.

 IV.    CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, the Michigan Attorney General requests that the Commission
deny SIGE’s Complaint, with or without prejudice. In the alternative, the Michigan Attorney
General requests that the Commission direct MISO to incorporate changes to the cost recovery
mechanism as discussed above.

from 11:59 PM Eastern Standard Time (EST) on December 23, 2025, until 11:59 PM Eastern

        Pursuant to the Federal Power Act (“the Act”) and Department procedures applying it to

petitions for rehearing, the States hereby file this timely request for rehearing of DOE’s Schahfer and

Culley Orders. Some of the States have already sought both rehearing and review of three similar orders that the

                                       MOTION TO INTERVENE

       The States2 move to intervene in this proceeding and thereby to become parties for

purposes of Section 313l of the Act, 16 U.S.C. § 825l. The States have an interest in and are

aggrieved by the subject orders (Exs. A, B) in several ways and seek to intervene and petition for

rehearing. FDR v. R.J. Reynolds Vapor Co., 606 U. S. ___ (2025) (slip op., at 3–8) (defining an

“adversely affected or aggrieved” party within the APA as “anyone even ‘arguably within the zone

of interests to be protected or regulated by the statute . . . in question.’” (quoting Association of

Data Processing Service Organizations, Inc. v. Camp, 397 U. S. 150, 153 (1970))).

       Factual Background

       The utilities regulated by the States are members of MISO, the electric grid operator for

the central United States. MISO covers the largest geographical range of any independent system

operator (“ISO”) in the U.S. The 15 states covered by MISO are: Arkansas, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa,

Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, North Dakota, South

Dakota, Texas, and Wisconsin. As the ISO of the electric grid in this region, MISO manages the

flow of electricity across the high-voltage, long-distance power lines. To do so, MISO develops

rules so that the wholesale electricity transmission system operates reliably and safely. MISO has

described this as being like the “air traffic controller” for the grid in its territory, 3 meaning that

MISO seeks to resolve power congestion (traffic) issues in real-time through its control room and

has processes in place to anticipate and avoid emergencies that could lead to the loss of power.

       The Orders direct MISO, in coordination with NIPSCO (Schahfer) and CenterPoint

(Culley), the respective operators of the plants, to ensure that the plants remain available for

operation during the period of the order (December 23, 2025, through March 23, 2026). Id.

       These eleventh-hour Orders disrupted a longstanding planning sequence handled by state

authorities and submitted to MISO, which included plans to retire the Schahfer and Culley Unit 2

plants on December 31, 2025.4 Ex. C (NIPSCO IRP). The integrated resource planning process

already accounted for increased need and slated adequate generation to meet requirements. Ex. C

at 6 (“Thus, the 2024 IRP was structured to ensure a robust assessment of the type of resources

needed to respond to emerging market conditions and future portfolio retirements.”). As recently

as October 29, 2025, NIPSCO recommitted to Indiana regulators its plan to retire Schahfer Units

17 and 18 in accordance with its January 2023 submission to MISO, which MISO approved in

February 2023. Ex. E.

       All three units at these two plants were slated for retirement because they are old and in

disrepair, and the units experienced deferred maintenance leading up to their planned retirement;

they cannot be economically operated and require significant overhaul and upkeep costs to stay

running. For example, CenterPoint explained that the Culley Unit 2 retirement was part of a plan

         Adverse Effects

        The States will be adversely affected by the Orders directed to the Schahfer and Culley

coal units in many of the same ways that they were harmed by the Campbell Orders that they have

separately requested rehearing or otherwise challenged.

        The Schahfer and Culley Orders prevent the planned retirement of the respective plants

with consequent negative impacts on the States.

        First, households and businesses in the States, and the States as consumers in their own

right, will pay higher electricity bills as a result of the Orders’ imposition of costs and cost-recovery

to the States. By ordering the utilities to take all steps necessary to make the coal plants available

and ordering MISO to take all steps necessary for the plants to provide economic dispatch, costs

are already being incurred and more costs will continue to be generated.

        Notably, the age of the units is concerning for costs, especially given the cost-savings

assessments of the retirement plans. The Orders will likely require at least a portion of capital

expenditures and major maintenance costs, which will drive up costs and impact ratepayer bills.

This would be in addition to the cost of rehiring operators and obtaining more coal, among other

expenses.

        Although the precise amount is not yet known, the Orders provide that cost recovery is

available through Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) proceedings. Exs. A-B at ¶E.

The operators have already initiated cost recovery complaints before FERC that, if approved, will

impact ratepayers on the States.

        Second, the States will suffer environmental harms as a result of the Order. The coal

operations at Schahfer and Culley are a significant source of particulate matter, nitrogen oxides,




                                                       7
 sulfur oxides, and carbon dioxide,5 among other pollutants. By extending the operations of the

plants beyond their planned retirement dates, the Orders increase the amount of pollution emitted

in the region, causing harm to the public health and welfare. 6 The States of Minnesota, Illinois,

Michigan, and Wisconsin share the upper Midwest region and Great Lakes environment with

Indiana. Depending on weather, air emissions in Indiana impact conditions in the States. Further,

        F.      The Orders are unreasoned, arbitrary, and capricious because their directive
               for “economic dispatch” is inherently contradictory with the needs to meet

       Section 202(c) contemplates emergency orders that are tailored to the specific

emergency—they must “best meet the emergency and serve the public interest.” 16 U.S.C. §

824a(c). Even if an emergency did exist and DOE had the legal authority to issue an order, these

two Orders are not rationally related to address the emergency that the Orders identify.

       The Orders’ specific requirement for MISO to take steps to effectuate “economic dispatch”

of the Schahfer and Culley coal units undermines their determination that an emergency exists and

cannot “best meet” the purported emergency. Economic dispatch is a term of art for the procedure

by which MISO selects generators to add electric energy to the grid. It is designed to ensure that

the electricity generated matches the demand in its service area in the most cost-effective way.

“Economic dispatch,” by definition, is awarded to the lowest-cost option (all else being equal). Ex.

Z. That is because much of the base load planning takes place years or months ahead of time and

is comprised of the must-run units. Additional capacity is then called upon in the day-ahead or

day-of markets for which additional generation is required:

identified and scheduled the day before, based upon the day-ahead load forecast used in the

security-constrained unit commitment process. Ex. AA at 6-7, 13, 51. As recently as 2021, the vast

majority of peaking plants operated on natural gas and oil which can be dispatched in much shorter

order; only 3.3 percent of all peakers nationwide burned coal. See Ex. BB at 2.

       Taken together, economic dispatch considers a variety of factors including (1) the cost of

generation, (2) the standby condition of the generator, (3) ramp-up time to provide the needed

capacity, and (4) whether electric energy can be transmitted to the area of need.

       The Orders’ proposed solution for “economic dispatch” of the Schahfer and Culley coal

units is thus inherently incompatible with addressing emergency operation (likely because there is

no emergency in the first place). In a true emergency, even uneconomic plants receive cost-of-

does not require the emergency generator to bid into the market and then make a determination
